title: Evaluating the Impact of Fertilizer Subsidy on Crop Yields

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy

**Method: Difference-in-Differences (DID)**

The data structure is a classic DID setup with:
- **Treatment group**: Farmers receiving the fertilizer subsidy (`treated = 1`)
- **Control group**: Farmers not receiving the subsidy (`treated = 0`)
- **Pre/post periods**: `post = 0` (before subsidy) and `post = 1` (after subsidy)
- **Interaction term**: `treat_x_post` captures the causal effect of the subsidy

The DID model is: `y = β₀ + β₁·treated + β₂·post + β₃·treat_x_post + ε`

where **β₃** is the Average Treatment Effect on the Treated (ATT) — the causal impact of the fertilizer subsidy on log crop yields.

**Key Assumption: Parallel Trends** — In the absence of the subsidy program, treated and control farmers would have experienced the same average change in log crop yields over time. This is plausible if the subsidy assignment was not based on differential productivity trends.

## 2. R Code

```r
# Load libraries
library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)

# Read data
df <- read.csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s50_data.csv")

# Explore data structure
cat("=== Data Summary ===\n")
cat("Dimensions:", nrow(df), "x", ncol(df), "\n")
cat("Observations by group:\n")
print(table(Treated = df$treated, Post = df$post))

cat("\n=== Group Means ===\n")
group_means <- aggregate(y ~ treated + post, data = df, FUN = mean)
print(group_means)

# Manual DID calculation
y_00 <- mean(df$y[df$treated == 0 & df$post == 0])  # Control, Pre
y_01 <- mean(df$y[df$treated == 0 & df$post == 1])  # Control, Post
y_10 <- mean(df$y[df$treated == 1 & df$post == 0])  # Treated, Pre
y_11 <- mean(df$y[df$treated == 1 & df$post == 1])  # Treated, Post

did_manual <- (y_11 - y_10) - (y_01 - y_00)
cat("\n=== Manual DID Calculation ===\n")
cat("Control Pre:", round(y_00, 4), "\n")
cat("Control Post:", round(y_01, 4), "\n")
cat("Treated Pre:", round(y_10, 4), "\n")
cat("Treated Post:", round(y_11, 4), "\n")
cat("Time trend (control):", round(y_01 - y_00, 4), "\n")
cat("Treated change:", round(y_11 - y_10, 4), "\n")
cat("DID estimate (manual):", round(did_manual, 4), "\n")

# ==========================================
# Main DID Regression
# ==========================================
cat("\n=== Main DID Regression (OLS) ===\n")
did_model <- lm(y ~ treated + post + treat_x_post, data = df)
summary(did_model)

# The key coefficient
att <- coef(did_model)["treat_x_post"]
cat("\n*** ATT (Fertilizer Subsidy Effect on Log Yields):", round(att, 4), "***\n")
cat("This implies a", round((exp(att) - 1) * 100, 2), "% change in crop yields.\n")

# ==========================================
# Robustness Check 1: Heteroskedasticity-robust SEs
# ==========================================
cat("\n=== Robustness: HC1 Robust Standard Errors ===\n")
robust_test <- coeftest(did_model, vcov = vcovHC(did_model, type = "HC1"))
print(robust_test)

# ==========================================
# Robustness Check 2: Wilcoxon rank-sum test on DID
# ==========================================
cat("\n=== Robustness: Non-parametric check ===\n")
# Compare changes: treated vs control (if panel structure allows)
# Since we have repeated cross-section style, compare post-period residualized outcomes
treated_post <- df$y[df$treated == 1 & df$post == 1]
control_post <- df$y[df$treated == 0 & df$post == 1]
treated_pre <- df$y[df$treated == 1 & df$post == 0]
control_pre <- df$y[df$treated == 0 & df$post == 0]

wilcox_result <- wilcox.test(treated_post, control_post)
cat("Wilcoxon test (post-period treated vs control): p-value =", round(wilcox_result$p.value, 4), "\n")

# ==========================================
# Robustness Check 3: Check for pre-treatment balance
# ==========================================
cat("\n=== Pre-Treatment Balance Check ===\n")
pre_test <- t.test(y ~ treated, data = df[df$post == 0, ])
cat("Pre-period mean difference (treated - control):", 
    round(pre_test$estimate[1] - pre_test$estimate[2], 4), "\n")
cat("t-test p-value:", round(pre_test$p.value, 4), "\n")
if (pre_test$p.value > 0.05) {
  cat("=> No significant pre-treatment difference (good for parallel trends)\n")
} else {
  cat("=> Significant pre-treatment difference detected (DID still valid if trends parallel)\n")
}

# ==========================================
# Robustness Check 4: Placebo test — effect in pre-period should be zero
# ==========================================
cat("\n=== Placebo: Treatment effect in pre-period only ===\n")
pre_only <- lm(y ~ treated, data = df[df$post == 0, ])
cat("Treated coefficient (pre-period only):", round(coef(pre_only)["treated"], 4), "\n")
cat("p-value:", round(summary(pre_only)$coefficients["treated", "Pr(>|t|)"], 4), "\n")
```

## 3. Expected Findings

- **Sign**: I expect the DID coefficient (`treat_x_post`) to be **positive**, indicating that the fertilizer subsidy increased crop yields. Fertilizer is a well-established productivity-enhancing input, and subsidies that increase its adoption should raise yields.

- **Magnitude**: Given that the outcome is in log yields, I expect the ATT to be in the range of **0.3–1.5 log points** (roughly 35–350% increase), though this depends on the simulation's data-generating process. A more realistic policy estimate would be 0.2–0.5 log points (~20–65% yield increase), which aligns with agricultural economics literature on input subsidy programs in developing countries.

- **Statistical significance**: With 25 observations per cell (100 total / 4 cells), significance depends on the effect size relative to variance. If the DGP includes a meaningful treatment effect, we should see significance at conventional levels (p < 0.05).

- **Robustness**: The HC1 robust standard errors should yield similar inference. The pre-treatment balance check should show no significant difference in levels between treated and control groups if the DGP is well-specified.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Compare changes in log crop yields over time between treated and untreated units.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The subsidy program significantly increased crop yields.
